passages.where: A sufferer cries out to a God who seems absent. The site's note points out that he does not doubt that God exists or that God is his; he asks why his God has left him. Jesus prayed this line from the cross, so the question of God and evil is one the Son of God himself spoke aloud.

After thirty-five chapters of argument, God speaks to Job out of the whirlwind, and he answers with questions, not an explanation. The reader was shown a scene in heaven at the start of the book that Job is never told. Job is a man suffering for a reason that exists and is never given to him, and God comes to him all the same.

God's verdict at the end falls on the friends who had explained Job's suffering as punishment, not on the man who had argued with God. They did not speak of God rightly, and Job did. Their sacrifice is accepted only when Job prays for them.

People bring Jesus the news of Galileans killed by Pilate, and he adds a disaster of his own: eighteen crushed when a tower fell. The note on the chapter draws the line plainly: cruelty and accident alike are no measure of the victims' guilt. Jesus turns the question from what they did to where each listener stands with God.

The disciples ask whose sin caused a man's blindness, and Jesus rejects both answers they offer. The site's plain note is firm that disability is not a punishment for sin, and that verse 3 does not mean God made a man blind for decades as a show. Jesus turns the question from who is to blame to what God will do here.

Jesus comes to the grave of his friend knowing he is about to raise him, and still he weeps with Mary and the mourners. Some who watched asked why the one who opened the eyes of the blind could not have kept this man from dying. John lets the question stand beside the tears.

Paul says the whole creation was subjected to futility and groans in bondage to decay. The note says the hope he names is not that God will discard the world but that he will set creation itself free. The present world is not as God means it to be, and Paul does not pretend that it is.

The speakers confess that they looked at the suffering Servant and assumed God was punishing him. Then they see what they missed: the sickness and sorrow he carried were theirs. Christians read the song as fulfilled in Christ, a God who does not stand outside suffering but carries it.

The book that opened with a complaint about violence ends with a prophet still trembling, waiting for the day of distress. Every crop and every flock may fail, and he resolves to rejoice in the God of his salvation anyway. It is faith that has looked at the worst and stayed.

The Bible's last picture is of God making his home with people and wiping away every tear himself. Death, mourning, crying and pain are named one by one as things that will pass away. The promise does not explain evil; it says how its story ends.

misread.taken: Older translations have God say that he creates evil, and the verse is sometimes used to teach that God is the author of wickedness, or, from the other side, as proof that the God of the Bible cannot be good.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter explains that the Hebrew word here means calamity or disaster, the opposite of well-being in the same line, not moral wickedness. God is speaking through Isaiah to Cyrus, the king he has raised up, about the rise and fall of nations, Babylon's fall among them, and claiming that no rival power can overturn his purpose. The note adds that Scripture elsewhere insists that God is not the author of sin (James 1:13), and that the verse was meant as comfort, not as an explanation of every evil.

whole: The question usually arrives with a name attached. A child with cancer, a friend killed on an ordinary road, a cruelty that made the news, a prayer that was not answered. If God is good and able to stop it, why did he not? Thoughtful unbelievers press the question honestly, and many believers carry it quietly, afraid that asking it is a betrayal. It is the strongest reason people give for not believing, and the Christian who has never felt its weight has probably not looked very long at the world.

Scripture does not treat the question as forbidden. It hands it to us in Job's speeches, in Habakkuk's complaint, in the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross, and in the martyrs under the altar asking how long. It names the deepest cause plainly: the world is not as God made it to be. Creation groans, human hearts turn against God and against each other, and much of the evil we suffer is evil people do. Yet the Bible also refuses the explanation people most often reach for. Job's friends said suffering tracks guilt, and God said they were wrong. Jesus said the people under the tower were no worse than anyone else, and that a man's blindness was not a punishment. The Bible gives no one leave to read a verdict in another person's pain, and that includes us, who have often done it.

That is where wisdom begins, and it begins humbly. It admits that we are not told most of the reasons. Job suffered for a reason that existed and was never given to him, and God came to him without supplying it. Wisdom does not stand back because God has purposes; Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty and spent his days healing what was broken, and his people are meant to resist evil the same way. It brings the protest to God rather than swallowing it, since lament is a form of faith, not its opposite. And it holds two things the church has always confessed together: that God is good and is not the author of sin, and that nothing in all creation is outside his rule.

The Christian answer is finally not an argument but an event. The God who could have explained evil from a distance came inside it instead. The Son was despised and rejected, carried sorrows that were not his, cried out the first line of Psalm 22, and died. If he was raised, then evil is real and it will not win. The last page of the Bible does not tell anyone why their particular suffering came. It tells them who will wipe away the tears, and that the hands that do it still bear the wounds.

differ.share: Christians agree that God is wholly good, that he is not the author of sin or a tempter to it, that human beings are truly responsible for the evil they do, that nothing is outside God's rule, that evil is real and will be judged, and that Christ's death and resurrection are God's answer to it. The site's notes on Genesis 50 and Isaiah 45 set out how they differ, and take no side.

views.name: God ordains all that comes to pass
views.body: The Reformed tradition teaches that God ordains all that comes to pass, even evil acts, without being the author of sin and without taking away human guilt. Joseph's brothers meant evil and were guilty, and God meant the same events for good. Holders of this view find comfort in knowing that no evil is outside God's purpose.

views.name: God permits what he does not will
views.body: The Arminian tradition teaches that God gives people real freedom, permits evil acts he does not will, and then overrules what they do for good. Holders of this view find comfort in knowing that God never wills the evil done to them, and that he is at work to bring good out of it.

differ.after: Both agree on what Genesis 50:20 says: the brothers were guilty, and God's good purpose was not defeated. The Honest Answer “Does God choose us, or do we choose him?” sets out the larger question.

sit: If you were never told why, what would you still want to say to God about it, and could you say it to him today?

prayer.lead: Psalm 13 asks how long four times before it turns to trust. Pray all of it, even if you can only mean the first half today.
